paragraphs: Fyodor Pavlovitch, by the way, had not been living in our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife’s death he had gone to the south of Russia and finally turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. At first, in his own words, he made the acquaintance “of a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and he ended by being received by “Jews high and low alike.” We may presume that in this period he developed a peculiar knack for making and hoarding money. He finally returned to our town only three years before Alyosha’s arrival. His old acquaintances found him looking terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man. He behaved not exactly with more dignity, but with more effrontery. The former buffoon now showed an insolent urge to make buffoons of others. His depravity with women was not just what it used to be, but even more revolting. In a short time he opened a great number of new taverns in the district. It was evident that he had perhaps a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many of the inhabitants of the town and district were soon in his debt, and, of course, had given good security. Lately, too, he looked somehow bloated, and seemed more irresponsible and unsteady. He had sunk into a sort of incoherence, would begin one thing and go on with another, as though he were letting himself go altogether. He was drunk more and more often. And if it had not been for the same servant Grigory, who by that time had aged considerably too, and who looked after him sometimes almost like a tutor, Fyodor Pavlovitch might have got into terrible scrapes. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to affect even his moral side, as though something had awakened in this prematurely old man that had long been dead in his soul.

“Do you know,” he often used to say, looking at Alyosha, “you’re like her, ‘the crazy woman’”—that was what he called his dead wife, Alyosha’s mother. It was Grigory who pointed out the “crazy woman’s” grave to Alyosha. He took him to our town cemetery and showed him, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone, cheap but decently kept. On it were inscribed the name and age of the deceased and the date of her death, and below them a four-line verse, of the kind commonly used on old-fashioned middle-class tombs. To Alyosha’s amazement, it turned out that Grigory had put up this tomb. He had set it on the poor “crazy woman’s” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he had often pestered about the grave, had gone to Odessa, abandoning the grave and all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother’s grave. He only listened to Grigory’s minute and solemn account of how the tomb was put up; he stood with bowed head and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he visited the cemetery again. But this little episode was not without an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for the soul of his wife. But they were not for the second wife, Alyosha’s mother, the “crazy woman,” but for the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, who used to thrash him. That evening he got drunk and abused the monks to Alyosha. He himself was far from religious; he had probably never put so much as a penny candle before the image of a saint. Strange impulses of sudden feeling and sudden thought are common in such men.

I have mentioned already that he looked bloated. His face at this time bore traces of something that showed unmistakably the life he had led. There were long fleshy bags under his little eyes, which were always insolent, suspicious, and ironical. There were deep wrinkles all over his small fat face. The Adam’s apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, which gave him a peculiar, repulsive, sensual look. Add to that a long, rapacious mouth with full lips, between which showed little stumps of black, decayed teeth. He slobbered every time he began to speak. He was fond, in fact, of making fun of his own face, though, I believe, he was well satisfied with it. He liked especially to point to his nose, which was not very large, but very delicate and conspicuously aquiline. “A regular Roman nose,” he used to say, “and with my goiter I have quite the look of an ancient Roman patrician of the decadent period.” He seemed proud of it.

Not long after visiting his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were willing to take him as a novice. He explained that this was his strong desire, and that he was solemnly asking his father’s consent. The old man knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“He’s the most honest monk among them, of course,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, and seeming scarcely surprised at the request. “H’m!... So that’s where you want to be, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he grinned his slow, half-drunken grin, which had a certain cunning and tipsy slyness to it. “H’m!... I had a feeling you’d end up in something like this. Would you believe it? You were heading straight for it. Well, to be sure, you have your own two thousand. That’s a dowry for you. And I’ll never desert you, my angel. And I’ll pay whatever’s needed for you there, if they ask for it. But if they don’t ask, why should we bother them? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. H’m!... Do you know that near one monastery there’s a place outside the town where every baby knows there’s nobody living but ‘the monks’ wives,’ as they’re called? Thirty women, I believe. I’ve been there myself. You know, it’s interesting in its own way, of course, for a change. The worst of it is, it’s awfully Russian. There are no French women there. Of course they could get them quick enough, they have plenty of money. If they hear of it, they’ll come along. Well, there’s nothing of that sort here, no ‘monks’ wives,’ and two hundred monks. They’re honest. They keep the fasts. I admit it.... H’m.... So you want to be a monk? And do you know, I’m sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I’ve really grown fond of you? Well, it’s a good opportunity. You’ll pray for us sinners; we’ve sinned too much here. I’ve always been wondering who would pray for me, and whether there’s anyone in the world who would. My dear boy, I’m awfully stupid about that. You wouldn’t believe it. Awfully. You see, however stupid I am about it, I keep thinking, I keep thinking—from time to time, of course, not all the while. It’s impossible, I think, for the devils to forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. Then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? What of? Iron hooks? Where do they forge them? Have they got a foundry down there of some sort? The monks in the monastery probably believe there’s a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now I’m ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. It makes it more refined, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And after all, what does it matter whether it has a ceiling or hasn’t? But, do you know, there’s a damnable question tied up in it? If there’s no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, it all falls apart, which is unlikely again, for then there’d be nobody to drag me down to hell, and if they don’t drag me down, what justice is there in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, on purpose for me alone, for if you only knew, Alyosha, what a blackguard I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” Alyosha said, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That’s how a Frenchman described hell: ‘_J’ai vu l’ombre d’un cocher qui avec l’ombre d’une brosse frottait l’ombre d’une carrosse._’ How do you know there are no hooks, darling? When you’ve lived with the monks you’ll sing a different tune. But go and get at the truth there, and then come and tell me. Anyway, it’s easier going to the other world if one knows what’s there. Besides, it’ll be more fitting for you with the monks than here with me, with a drunken old man and young harlots ... though you’re like an angel, nothing touches you. And I expect nothing will touch you there either. That’s why I’m letting you go, because I hope for that. You’ve got all your wits about you. You’ll burn and you’ll burn out; you’ll be healed and come back again. And I’ll wait for you. I feel that you’re the only creature in the world who hasn’t condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can’t help feeling it.”
And he actually started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.
